newsitem.title: UK: British union boss reminds Labour to help the weak.
newsitem.headline: British union boss reminds Labour to help the weak.

text.p: The leader of Britain's trade unions applauded the Labour Party's huge election win on Friday but said the unions expected the new government to give greater protection to the more vulnerable sections of society.
John Monks, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), shares a similar approach to Labour leader Tony Blair, who has discarded many of the Party's socialist principles.
But Blair has also scrapped some of Labour's traditional promises to the unions.

In particular, he has discarded a commitment to extend legal protections and minimum rights to all workers from their first day in a job -- a particular source of friction, even with the mild-mannered Monks.

"At the moment you've got to work two years before you get protection from unfair dismissal. We know Mr Blair has said it wasn't going to be day one rights, but we think the present qualifying period is far, far too long," Monks told Reuters.
"We'll certainly be raising that with the government and seeking the inclusion of more of the vulnerable workers within employment protection legislation."
Before former Conservative premier Margaret Thatcher took power in 1979 workers had to work for six months before gaining protection. She extended the period to two years.
"I think that was a pretty mean and malicious act aimed at some of the weakest in our society...We would like that back," Monks said.
Monks has modernised the TUC over the past four years and, like Blair, has strived to find common ground with industry.
"Removing the business community's suspicions about the Labour Party has been one of the triumphs of the new Labour regime," he said.
"We're keen to see Labour have a good relationship with the business community -- not at our expense, but we're keen to see social partnership develop in Britain," he added.
Applauding Labour's "absolutely tremendous victory", Monks played down worries that an upsurge in union militancy would inevitably follow from the Labour landslide.
"There isn't necessarily going to be a wage push. Low inflation has been around for some time, it's very important that we keep it. The TUC is as keen on that as anybody else."
Blair is committed to ending Britain's opt-out from the Social Chapter, which provides a framework for minimum employment rights in Europe.
Monks said he was not too concerned by comments made by Labour leaders during the election campaign that European social rules should not be allowed to undermine the competitveness of British firms.
"I'm sure the Labour message will be that they want flexibility, but they want fairness as well."

Blair has made it clear he would not repeal the employment laws brought in by the Conservatives since 1979 that severely restricted union activities, in the process cutting the number of days lost through strikes in the 1990s to historic lows.

The union leadership has accepted defeat here, and Monks said his demands related mostly to what was in Labour's "ambitious" manifesto -- the introduction of a minimum wage, signing the Social Chapter and a new right to union representation if workers voted for it.
"We don't expect any turning the clocks back, any massive changes in union law, but we would expect what is in the manifesto," he said.
($ = 0.616 British Pounds)
